procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 2nd August, 1983 (rejecting application to dismiss the Election Petition) and Judgment and Order dated the 15th October, 1982 and 1st December, 1982 in Election Petition No. 1 of 1982.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The 1st Respondent filed separate Election Petitions in the High Court to set aside the election of the appellants to the Rajya Sabha. An application was filed to dismiss the Election Petition, which the High Court rejected.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals were made to the Supreme Court by Special Leave. The main point raised by the appellant was that two sets of copies were filed by the election-petitioner in the High Court, one set being a correct and exact one and the other.

directions: The judgment of the High Court is set aside.
The election petitions are dismissed in limine under s.86 of the Act.
There will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether an election petition is liable to be dismissed in limine under Section 86 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for non-compliance with Section 81(3) of the Act, where the original petition filed in court was missing a page that was present in the copies served on the respondents.

facts: An election petition was filed to set aside the election of the appellants.
The original petition filed in court was missing page 17.
However, the copies of the petition that were served on the appellants (the respondents in the election petition) did contain the missing page 17.
The election petitioner later sought and was granted an amendment by the High Court to insert the missing page 17 into the original petition.
The appellants argued that the petition should be dismissed at the outset (in limine) because the copies served were not true copies of the original petition as it was initially filed.
law: Section 81(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, requires that every copy of an election petition served on a respondent must be a "true and exact copy" of the original petition.
Section 86 of the Act mandates that the High Court shall dismiss an election petition which does not comply with the provisions of Section 81.
The Supreme Court has held that the requirement under Section 81(3) is a "peremptory provision" (mandatory), and total non-compliance will result in the dismissal of the petition under Section 86.
application: The Court reasoned that based on the "admitted position" that the original petition lacked page 17 while the served copies contained it, the copies served on the appellants were not "correct and exact copies" of the election petition.
The Court held that the mandatory provisions of Section 81(3) could not be bypassed or cured by a subsequent amendment to the original petition. The compliance must be met at the time of filing.
The Court emphasized that it is the duty of the election petitioner to ensure that the copy served is a correct one. If there is a discrepancy, it amounts to non-compliance with Section 81(3).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the election petition was liable to be dismissed in limine under Section 86 of the Act. The failure to serve a true copy of the original petition, due to the discrepancy of the missing page, constituted a fatal non-compliance with the mandatory requirement of Section 81(3), which could not be rectified by a later amendment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the requirement under Section 81(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, that every copy of the election petition must be a true and exact copy of the original, is a mandatory provision, the non-compliance of which cannot be cured by amendment or excused on the grounds of being a technical objection that caused no prejudice.

facts: An election petition was filed against the appellant, who then sought its dismissal under Section 86 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
The appellant's ground for dismissal was that the copy of the petition served on him was not a true and exact copy of the original, as required by Section 81(3) of the Act.
The election petitioner admitted that multiple sets of copies were filed, some correct and some incorrect, or that the copies served contained a page that was missing from the original petition.
The petitioner argued that the defect could be cured by amendment.
law: The Court examined Section 81(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which requires that every copy of an election petition served on a respondent must be a true and exact copy of the original.
It also considered Section 86 of the Act, which mandates the dismissal of an election petition for non-compliance with Section 81.
application: The Court held that the language of Section 81(3) is a "clear and specific" and "peremptory provision" that must be strictly followed.
It is the duty of the election petitioner to ensure that the copy served on the respondent is correct. If the petitioner files incorrect copies, they risk having the petition dismissed at the outset.
The Court reasoned that allowing a petitioner to cure such a defect through amendment would "defeat the very object and purpose" of the mandatory requirement in Section 81(3).

The Court found that a discrepancy between the original petition and the copy served (such as a missing or extra page) is a significant inconsistency and constitutes a total non-compliance with the law.

Citing precedent, the Court noted that even smaller errors, like a missing signature on the attestation, have been held to be fatal, making the substantial inconsistencies in this case even more serious.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the requirement under Section 81(3) is a mandatory provision. The failure to serve a true and exact copy of the election petition is a fatal defect that cannot be cured by amendment and requires the dismissal of the election petition under Section 86 of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an election petition is liable to be dismissed in limine under Section 86 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for non-compliance with Section 81(3) of the Act, where the original petition filed in court was missing a page that was present in the copies served on the respondents.
appellant_arguments: The non-compliance with Section 81(3) results in an invalidity of the election petition that cannot be cured, thus mandating its dismissal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent factually rebutted the charge, claiming that the appellant had received a correct copy as required by the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the requirement under Section 81(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, that every copy of the election petition must be a true and exact copy of the original, is a mandatory provision, the non-compliance of which cannot be cured by amendment or excused on the grounds of being a technical objection that caused no prejudice.
appellant_arguments: The argument that no prejudice was caused is 'beside the point' and does not cure the invalidity of the election petition, as the provision is mandatory.
respondent_arguments: The objection is 'highly technical' and should be excused because it did not cause any prejudice to the appellants.
The non-compliance can be cured by invoking the 'doctrine of benefit-of-doubt'.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The mandatory provisions of Section 81(3) of the Act, which require the filing of correct copies of an election petition, must be strictly complied with, and any failure to do so will result in the dismissal of the petition in limine under Section 86 of the Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 81(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is a peremptory and mandatory provision. Total non-compliance with this provision, such as serving an incorrect copy of the election petition on a respondent, is a fatal defect that cannot be cured. Such non-compliance requires the dismissal of the election petition in limine under Section 86 of the Act. The petitioner who files incorrect copies takes the risk of the petition being dismissed, and it is not the duty of the respondent to search through the record to find the correct copy.
legal_tests_applied: Strict Compliance for Mandatory Provisions: The court applied a test of strict compliance for what it deemed a 'peremptory provision' of election law. Under this test, 'total non-compliance' with the provision automatically entails the statutory consequence of dismissal under Section 86.

Rejection of Curative Doctrines: The court explicitly rejected the application of the 'doctrine of benefit-of-doubt' to cure the non-compliance of a mandatory provision, stating that to do so would defeat the very object and purpose of Section 81(3).
policy_considerations: Statutory Nature of Election Law: The court emphasized that an election dispute is not a common law action but is purely a creature of statute. Therefore, the procedural requirements laid out by the law, which mandate time-bound disposal, must be strictly followed.

Importance of Timely Resolution: The court reasoned that the object of the Act is to avoid any 'halt or arrest in progress of the case,' as this would frustrate the goal of having duly elected representatives available to discharge their duties in a parliamentary democracy.

Primacy of Procedure and Rule of Precedent: The court acknowledged the harshness of its ruling, noting that it 'restores that primacy of procedure over justice' and makes Section 86(1) a 'tyrannical master.' However, it felt bound by the 'rigidity of the rule of precedent' and stated that any change to this balance is a matter for Parliament to address.
